Reflexive pronouns are pronouns that end in -self or -selves. A reflexive pronoun is used to refer back to the subject of the sentence or clause in which it appears.

sentences.text: We helped ourselves to more soup.
The reflexive pronoun, ourselves, refers back to the subject, we.
After the guests left, Amy made herself a cup of tea.
The reflexive pronoun, herself, refers back to the subject Amy.

header.text: A reflexive pronoun should only be used to refer to the subject of the sentence or clause in which it appears. To refer to someone else or something else, a personal pronoun, like me, you, him, her, it, us, or them, should be used instead.

sentences.text: Jake wrote a note for himself.
The reflexive pronoun, himself, refers back to the subject, Jake.
Jake wrote a note for him.
The personal pronoun, him, must refer to someone other than the subject, Jake.

A subject pronoun acts as the subject of a sentence or clause. It can also act as a predicate nominative, following a linking verb (like am, is, are, was, were, or be). The main subject pronouns are I, you, he, she, it, we, and they.

sentences.text: Ryan is out of town, but he can be reached by phone or email.
The subject pronoun he is the subject of a clause.
Yes, it was she who won first place.
The subject pronoun she is a predicate nominative. It follows the linking verb was.

header.text: An object pronoun acts as the object of an action verb or preposition (like at, for, on, of, to, or with). The main object pronouns are me, you, him, her, it, us, and them.

sentences.text: "No one appreciates me!" lamented Tracy.
The object pronoun me is the direct object of the action verb appreciates.
Dr. Yang showed us the X-ray.
The object pronoun us is the indirect object of the action verb showed.
The phone call was for him.
The object pronoun him is the object of the preposition for.
